description: Soy docente de Educación tecnológica y estoy en este espacio con ganas de aprender y de sumar nuevas herramientas. Mi idea es poder usar la IA y los recursos digitales para armar clases más actualizadas, dinámicas y divertidas, que realmente conecten con mis estudiantes y les den ganas de participar.
summary:
This project brings 1st-year students (13 years old) from School No. 59 in El Impenetrable, Chaco, closer to historical NASA missions (Spirit and Opportunity on Mars, the Dawn probe at Vesta and Ceres, and Pioneer 10, heading towards the stars) through an interactive web and mobile experience that bridges them with the legends of the Wichí worldview. 

It is important because in this community in the heart of El Impenetrable, the stories of the land and the forest have a direct bridge to space: the origin of water, shared fire, and the path of the constellations, joining their native Wichí language with the scientific exploration of the universe.
details:
What did we do and how does it work? 

We created ORBITA 59, an interactive web and mobile educational experience designed specifically for 13-year-old students (1st year of Basic Cycle) at School No. 59 in El Impenetrable, Chaco (Argentina). Instead of creating a traditional webpage read from top to bottom, we inverted the navigation: the journey starts at the very bottom, at the roots of a giant Yuchán (silk floss tree), and students gently "climb" upwards until reaching the starry sky.

As they climb up the tree, they pass through 3 levels, and in each level two worlds meet face to face, united by a common idea:

Level 1 (Water):

On the left, "The Legend of the Yuchán — The Origin of the Waters" (adapted through a dialogue between a grandfather and his grandson under a palo santo tree, accompanied by the audio recording of the original legend in the historical native Wichí language and real photos of silk floss trees in front of the National Historic Monument "La Misión" in Misión Nueva Pompeya).

On the right, the mission of NASA's twin rovers Spirit and Opportunity, which traversed the dry desert of Mars searching for traces of ancient rivers and lakes.

Level 2 (Fire and Light):

On the left, the Wichí story "When Animals Could Talk — The Rabbit and the Fire"

(with original audio in the Wichí language and illustrations by Lorena Leonhardt), where the little Chaco rabbit dares to carry a small ember that the jaguar refused to share, hiding the fire inside the wood of the trees.

On the right, NASA's Dawn mission: a small spacecraft powered by an ion engine glowing like a small blue ember in the dark, traveling alone to Vesta and Ceres to share knowledge with everyone, and today quietly orbiting Ceres like an ember that has already shared its fire.

Level 3 (The Path to the Stars):

On the left, the Wichí story about Chelchupé (the Pleiades) and Nayic (the white path of the sky connected to the forest with chaguar fibers).

On the right, NASA's Pioneer 10 probe, carrying the Golden Plaque with a greeting from a man and a woman heading toward Aldebaran, near the Pleiades.

Each time a student opens and reads a story, that card or star becomes "painted" with color on the tree until all 6 stories are completed and they reach the celestial canopy.

What did we consider and what impact did we seek? 

We worked with a concrete reality: in El Impenetrable, students rarely have good internet access, use basic smartphones, and are not familiar with technical or English vocabulary. Therefore, we made very specific decisions:

Pedagogical and cultural adaptation: We adapted the stories respecting the culture of the Wichí people and the age of the students (13 years old), without using English words in the buttons or interface.

Preservation of territory and living Wichí language: With the collaboration of teacher Valeria Inés Couseiro (from Misión Nueva Pompeya) and the voice of Berté Simeón (an ICT Teaching student in Misión Nueva Pompeya), we included audio narrations in the native historical Wichí language maintained by the community, alongside real photographs taken at the "La Misión" National Historic Monument (declared National Heritage in 1989, the first construction in El Impenetrable).

Technical optimization for low signal and mobile devices: We developed the site in pure HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript (without heavy frameworks), featuring a smooth scrolling system for mobile phones, background locking while reading stories, and processed audio files with ffmpeg and a Web Audio API voice booster (🔊 Boost voice volume), reducing files from over 4 MB to under 950 KB and 470 KB so they load quickly and play loudly on any phone.
